# Mustafa Hafeez

Mustafa joined Visokio in 2007 and is now a senior software engineer working on Omniscope, a data analytics platform. Independent developer of Travel Document Vault, an offline app for passports, visas and IDs. His writing draws on practical work with product features, automation, AI integrations and releases. He offers independent technical consultancy on reporting, integrations, automation and practical AI.

# How I’m building verification into AI\-assisted development

Turning engineering experience into a Definition of Done: tests, review perspectives and evidence for accepting AI\-assisted work\.

By Mustafa Hafeez · 2026-11-15

These are my personal views and experiences\. They do not represent the views of Visokio or any other organisation\.

## The takeaway

Choose inputs and observations that can expose a mistake, record what actually ran and keep untested behaviour visible\.

![A handmade paper bridge with a section lifted out beside a measuring square\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/verification-ai-assisted-development-cover-v1.webp)

Conceptual illustration of inspecting work before accepting it\.

## An agent’s completion report leaves questions to answer

When an AI agent tells me a feature is finished, I want to know what it actually checked\. A passing test tells me something useful about the behaviour it exercised\. I still need to understand whether that behaviour matches what someone using the app needs\.

I’ve worked on software since 2007\. Building Travel Document Vault, my independent app, has given me a reason to turn that experience into explicit expectations that agents can follow\. Reporting a change as complete should mean supplying evidence for those expectations, including any checks that could not be completed\.

This is the role of my Definition of Done\. It brings together the questions I want answered before accepting a feature, from its calculations and error handling to usability and privacy\.

## The Definition of Done grows when a review exposes a gap

I’ve developed the process with AI agents as the app has grown\. Reviews have exposed gaps, including missing screen states and test data that could not distinguish the intended behaviour from a plausible alternative\. Each finding gives me a reason to reconsider what the completion evidence should contain\.

A useful addition explains what evidence would settle the question\. “Check the error handling” leaves a lot to interpretation\. Asking for the failure condition, the message shown and the route back to a usable state gives the review something concrete to examine\.

There is a maintenance cost here\. A growing checklist can become repetitive or stop matching the product\. I need to review the requirements too, particularly when a feature changes the assumptions behind an earlier check\.

## Test data must separate the right answer from a plausible one

Consider a fictional travel summary labelled “days used so far”\. Its calculation might accidentally include a future trip\. If the test data contains only past trips, the correct calculation and the faulty one return the same total\. A screenshot could look entirely reasonable\.

Add a future trip and the difference becomes visible\. The test can now ask whether the displayed total agrees with the label\. The dates, calculation and wording need to be examined together\.

This is the question I want the verification process to keep asking: what would make this result demonstrably wrong? More assertions against the same undemanding input may leave the original assumption untouched\.

![A fictional example: past\-only input gives the same total for both interpretations; adding a future trip exposes the difference\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/verification-ai-assisted-development-input-v1.svg)

The input needs to distinguish the intended behaviour from a plausible mistake\.

## Different checks need different evidence

Unit tests let me examine focused behaviour with controlled inputs\. End\-to\-end tests, including Detox, exercise journeys through the running app\. Visual review helps examine the screens and states presented along the way\. A result from one of these checks does not establish that the others ran\.

I also use simulated personas to review the experience from different perspectives\. A hurried person may struggle with a recovery step that seems obvious to someone carefully following instructions\. A cautious person may need clearer wording before continuing\. These reviews can suggest questions and reveal friction, but they are AI simulations, not research with real users\.

The evidence available to a reviewer matters\. A static capture can support a finding about visible wording or layout\. It cannot establish how a screen reader announces a control or whether an interaction works on a physical device\. Those need their own observations\.

Privacy is also an explicit review question\. The check needs to name the relevant data expectation and how it will be examined\. Listing privacy in the Definition of Done does not establish that a particular feature has satisfied it\.

## What I ask each verification layer to establish

This is how I organise the questions\. The completion record still needs to show which checks actually ran for a particular change\.

| Verification layer | Question I want answered | Evidence to look for | What it cannot establish alone |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit tests | Does the focused logic match the requirement? | Controlled inputs, expected values and actual results | A complete journey through the app |
| End\-to\-end tests | Can the relevant journey reach its intended outcome? | A run through the running app, including relevant failure paths | Behaviour outside that run’s inputs and environment |
| Visual review | Are the required states clear and readable? | Captures of the intended states, tied to the reviewed version | Interaction or screen\-reader behaviour from a still image |
| Simulated personas | Where might different perspectives reveal friction? | Questions and observations grounded in the available screens or journey | Evidence that real users succeed |
| Privacy review | Does the feature respect its stated data expectations? | A specific expectation and evidence of the relevant behaviour | Every security or misuse risk |
| Security review | Could a restriction be bypassed or information exposed? | Scoped checks, findings, fixes and unresolved risks | A guarantee of security or an independent audit |
| Device and acceptance review | Is there enough evidence to accept this change? | Relevant device observations and a record of remaining gaps | Behaviour on every device or in every situation |

## Security review asks how a feature could be misused

For me, security adds another question to the review: how could this feature be misused? A feature can behave as intended while allowing an action it should prevent\.

In a fictional document app, I would ask whether a restricted action is still rejected when the usual screen is bypassed, and whether an error message reveals information it should keep private\. Those questions need evidence of their own\.

I want security questions raised while the design can still change, followed by checks of the implementation and release\. When a finding leads to a fix, a repeatable regression test can help catch the same failure in later changes\. The record should say what was examined and what remains unresolved; an automated scan or an AI review should not be presented as an independent security audit\.

## Automation makes the checks repeatable and the gaps visible

For a solo developer, repeatedly holding every expectation in my head is a poor way to manage quality\. Writing those expectations down makes it possible for agents to run checks and return evidence in a form I can inspect\.

For the fictional travel summary, a completion record could start with the following fields\. The observation must come from the run; the expected result alone cannot fill it\.

The aim is to reduce repetitive checking and dependence on memory\. Acceptance still involves judgement\. Device behaviour, the quality of the test inputs and the meaning of a requirement can need further investigation even when automated checks pass\.

```
Illustrative completion record, not an executed test

Claim: the total counts only days already used.
Input: one completed trip and one future trip.
Expected: adding the future trip leaves the total unchanged.
Observed: record the actual output after running the check.
Version/environment: identify the change and test setup.
Unchecked: list behaviour this run did not exercise.
```

## An AI\-generated analysis also needs a route back to the evidence

The person accepting an AI\-generated analysis needs similar access to the logic and evidence behind it\. That connects my development checks with a different part of my work: analytics\.

At Visokio, where I work on Omniscope, the team’s verifiable analytics approach gives end users ways to do that\. Insight Explorer presents visual answers alongside inspectable queries and transformations\. People can examine calculations and query lineage, inspect the chart configuration and compare the result with the source data\.

For a fictional sales question, that might mean checking which records contributed to a regional total, which filters were applied and how the values were grouped\. A chart helps someone explore the breakdown while the underlying logic lets them challenge the calculation\. Useful work can remain available to edit and rerun\.

That gives the user a practical way to verify an answer before acting on it\. The assumptions and source data still need checking; the value is having access to the evidence needed to do so\.

## Choose one claim and try to disprove it

For your next AI\-assisted change, choose one claim you would otherwise accept from the completion report\. Find an input or observation that would expose a wrong interpretation\. Run the check against the actual change and record what remains untested\.

If the check cannot distinguish the intended behaviour from a plausible mistake, improve the input or the observation before adding more checks\. That is the kind of verification I want built into each feature: specific enough to catch a failure, repeatable where possible, and clear about what still needs attention\.

## Sources

- [Detox: testing interactions in a running React Native app](<https://wix.github.io/Detox/docs/introduction/getting-started/>)

- [Visokio: verifiable AI analytics across the data journey](<https://visokio.com/verifiable-ai-analytics-across-the-data-journey/?utm_source=mustafa_hafeez&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=personal_website&utm_content=verification_article>)

- [OWASP: Mobile Application Security Testing Guide](<https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/>)

[Read on the website](https://mustafahafeez.com/blog/verification-ai-assisted-development/)


# Your AI agent’s instructions grew while you weren’t looking

An instruction audit found ignored scope metadata, stale guidance and safeguards lost during trimming\. Five checks for reviewing what your agent reads\.

By Mustafa Hafeez · 2026-11-12

These are my personal views and experiences\. They do not represent the views of Visokio or any other organisation\.

## The takeaway

Measure what loads, verify scope and stale facts, and preserve obligations when trimming instructions\.

![An overflowing accordion folio spreads across a walnut desk while a hand selects a compact bound set of essential cards\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/ai-agent-context-cover.webp)

A conceptual illustration of accumulated instructions and a smaller core\.

## Instructions accumulate between tasks

While working with AI coding agents on an independent project, I approved a plan to reduce the instructions loaded into our sessions\. The audit had found something more specific than long files: rules intended for particular work were loading everywhere because their scope was written in a format the loader did not recognise\.

The files had grown through useful additions: a correction after a mistake, a procedure for the next task, a status note left for a later session\. Taken together, they mixed current obligations with history and stale facts\. I wanted a check that would stop the accumulation from happening again\.

The repair also introduced a problem\. An independent review found safeguards missing from the shortened instructions, along with wording that contradicted another rule\. Both needed correcting before the changes were committed\. That review shaped the advice below: measure what loads, but check what survives the edit\.

## Measure the baseline before changing it

We examined fresh\-session logs and listed the files loaded on every request, with their byte sizes\. That separated the size of our instruction files from the larger amount of context already present when work began\.

For your own check, start a fresh session and inspect the context breakdown before giving the agent a task, if your tool exposes one\. Record the tool version, enabled integrations and measurement point\. Then inventory the instructions that load unconditionally\. System instructions and tool information can also occupy context; the total is not a measurement of your prose alone\.

Repeat under the same conditions after an edit\. File bytes are useful for tracking growth, but they are not an exact token count\. If the baseline is already small and the instructions are current, this may reveal little worth changing\.

## Test whether scoped rules stay scoped

In our audit, some rules described their intended scope in ordinary prose instead of the metadata the tool parsed\. They were treated as unscoped\. Correcting that mattered more than tightening their sentences\.

Check your tool's current documentation before changing the format\. In a disposable session, read a harmless file outside the intended scope and inspect which rules loaded\. Use a separate fresh session to check a matching file\. A rule left in context by an earlier task can confuse the comparison\. Treat this as a proposed diagnostic, rather than a test I am claiming we performed in this form\.

We kept rules triggered by events in the core instructions\. A requirement that applies before a particular action still needs to be available when that action involves no matching project file\.

## Re\-test claims that a capability is unavailable

A separate incident exposed guidance saying a capability was unavailable\. A live check showed it worked\. We also corrected stale counts and names that were still being supplied as current information\.

Search for statements such as 'unsupported', 'broken' or 'disabled'\. Separate factual limitations from deliberate permission boundaries\. Verify a capability with a harmless, authorised check; an instruction forbidding an action is not permission to try it\.

For a count you keep, record how to reproduce it and when it was checked\. An incorrect claim that something works tends to produce a visible failure\. A claim that something cannot work may simply prevent anyone from trying it again\.

## Move detail without losing obligations

We separated always\-needed instructions from longer detail, moving text into separate files and leaving pointers behind\. Moving a file only helps if the tool does not automatically load the whole thing through that pointer; check its loading behaviour\.

The independent review then caught the lost safeguards and conflicting guidance\. A smaller file still needed a behavioural repair\.

Before trimming, list the obligations expressed by words such as 'must', 'always' and 'never'\. Afterwards, trace each one to its new location and check when it becomes available\. Search the remaining files for contradictions\. Ask a reviewer who did not make the edit to check that mapping\. Keyword searches are a starting point: a safeguard can be expressed without any of those words\.

![Paper models labelled Core rules, Task detail and Review the move show connected instructions and a hand comparing a checklist\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/ai-agent-context-inline.webp)

Keep the obligation available at the point where it applies\. This conceptual illustration shows a compact core, connected detail and a review of the move\.

## Enforce the budget and inspect the pressure

Advice to keep the files concise had not held\. We added an automated byte\-budget check that could fail before a commit, rather than relying on another reminder in the instructions\.

The main file later returned to its cap\. That is a reason to inspect what is competing for space\. Raising a limit may be justified, but first check whether old status notes or occasional procedures are displacing current rules\.

We also moved session state to disk and started fresh sessions at task boundaries\. That addresses accumulated conversation separately from persistent instructions\. A useful handover needs the current decision, unfinished work and checks still required; it should not become another unbounded history file\.

## Smaller context leaves other questions open

The session record reports smaller fixed context per request alongside higher total usage during a busier period with more requests\. It does not establish a cost saving\. Output quality was not measured, and the planned quality check was not recorded as completed\.

Start with one rule you believe is scoped\. Check when it loads, make one change, then repeat the observation and review the obligations\. If the rule was already loading correctly, or the relevant material still loads through another route, that would change the diagnosis\. Keep the resulting evidence alongside the instructions so the next edit has something concrete to compare\.

## Sources

- [Claude Code documentation: path\-specific rules and loading behaviour](<https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#path-specific-rules>)

- [Claude Code documentation: what occupies the context window](<https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works#the-context-window>)

[Read on the website](https://mustafahafeez.com/blog/ai-agent-context-instructions/)


# When an AI agent cannot run your tests

How I adapted tooling tests for a restricted environment, and why some checks still needed the real machine\.

By Mustafa Hafeez · 2026-11-10

These are my personal views and experiences\. They do not represent the views of Visokio or any other organisation\.

## The takeaway

Before replacing an external dependency with a fixture, identify the real behaviour each test must still observe\.

![A paper model testing station inside a transparent enclosure and a physical computer feed results towards a shared review notebook\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/agent-test-environments-cover.webp)

A conceptual illustration of testing inside a restricted environment and against the real machine\.

## The agent could edit the code, but the tests were blocked

Some tests in my app’s developer tooling worked on the real machine and failed to run inside the coding agent’s sandbox\. They needed access to process lists and local sockets that the restricted environment could not provide\.

I wanted the agent to check useful parts of its work before handing a change back\. Sending every verification run outside the sandbox would leave another person or agent to do it\.

I chose to adapt the tests that could run inside, while keeping checks of real\-machine behaviour in a separate host run\. During review, we found that some replacements had lost behaviour the original tests checked\.

## Two questions were being tested together

Consider a tool that checks whether a background process is running\. It has to obtain a process list from the operating system, then decide whether the process it wants appears in that list\.

Those are two questions\. Can the tool make the right decision from the information it receives? And can it get the right information from the machine?

Supplied test data, often called a fixture, can answer the first question\. Give the code a known list and check its decision\. This can run inside a restricted environment without inspecting the laptop’s other processes\.

The second question needs access to the real interaction\. A supplied list cannot tell us whether the operating\-system command works\.

## What a fixture can show

This teaching example uses invented process identifiers\. The function receives another function, listProcesses, which supplies the list\. That lets a test control the input without asking the operating system\.

```
function isRunning(pid, listProcesses) {
  return listProcesses().includes(pid);
}

isRunning(42, () => [42, 73]); // true
isRunning(42, () => [73]);     // false
```

## The real command could break while those tests passed

In the first call, the supplied list contains 42, so isRunning returns true\. The second list contains only 73, so it returns false\. Together they check the present and absent decisions\.

Both would keep passing if the real process\-list command stopped working\. Neither call uses it\. That missing interaction needs its own check, for example by starting a controlled process and verifying that the real observation can find it\.

There is another question to settle when reviewing code like this\. What happens if the process list is unavailable? Returning an empty list would make an observation failure look like an absent process\. The implementation needs an explicit way to handle that uncertainty\. This is a review question, rather than a further bug found in my tooling\.

## Review found what the replacements could no longer see

One replacement test asserted information it had constructed itself\. Another could only see processes it had already been told about, so a stray process could escape its view\.

Those findings changed the repair\. The original operating\-system checks were preserved in a separately named host\-only set\. Fixture\-based tests covered the decisions inside the sandbox\.

The comparison that helped was to ask what each old test observed and what its replacement could observe\. A similar assertion or a passing test count would have missed that difference\.

![Use sandbox fixtures to test decisions from known inputs\. Keep host integration checks for real system interactions\. Review both results\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/agent-test-environments-flow-v2.svg)

Fixture and host checks answer separate questions about the same implementation\.

## Both test runs needed a result

The recorded final checks passed for the targeted sandbox suites and the full host run\. Each result had a different scope\. The sandbox tests covered the selected decisions using controlled inputs, and the host run supplied the broader integration evidence\.

Keeping host checks separate creates an ongoing job\. They need a clear place in the review process, otherwise a move intended to make tests runnable can quietly leave some checks behind\.

A useful handover identifies which tests ran, where they ran, the revision and the result\. If a sandbox run excludes host\-only tests, its result needs the corresponding host result alongside it\.

## Ask what the test actually observes

Before replacing a dependency in a test, write down what the existing test can see\. Then ask whether the implementation could break while the replacement still passed\. Identify the check that would catch that failure and where it will run\.

A database gives another example\. A fake returned row can help test how code handles the data\. A separate integration test can establish whether the real query and connection work in the intended environment\.

In my tooling, fixtures made decision tests runnable inside the sandbox\. Keeping the host checks preserved the evidence about real process behaviour that the fixtures could not supply\.

## About this note

Based on my work adapting developer\-tooling tests for a restricted environment\. Implementation details are generalised, and the code example uses invented identifiers\.

## Sources

- [Jest documentation on replacing dependencies with mock data](<https://jestjs.io/docs/manual-mocks>)

[Read on the website](https://mustafahafeez.com/blog/tests-inside-agent-sandbox/)


# Before I accept an AI agent’s changes

Checking what my website build would publish, and how I tested an AI agent’s release check\.

By Mustafa Hafeez · 2026-11-09

These are my personal views and experiences\. They do not represent the views of Visokio or any other organisation\.

## The takeaway

Choose one failure the change must reject, demonstrate that rejection, and attach the result to the version being released\.

![Conceptual paper models of an app and websites bring work towards a human review desk and release gate\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/ai-agent-review-cover.webp)

A conceptual illustration of preparing work across an app and its websites\.

## A successful build left a question

While building this website with AI coding agents, I needed to keep drafts, build scripts and agent instructions private\. The finished pages belonged in a public repository\. The source belonged in a separate private one\.

A successful build could still copy an unwanted file into the public output\. Looking at the website in a browser would tell me whether the pages looked right\. It would leave a stray notes file sitting alongside those pages unseen\.

Agents helped implement the publishing checks\. Before accepting that work, I wanted to see what happened when the output contained something that had no reason to go live\.

## An approved list gave me something to compare

The build writes the public website into its own output directory\. The checker walks that directory, lists every file and compares the result with the files approved for release\. An unexpected file or a missing one stops the check\.

The complete inventory matters\. A list of forbidden names only covers names someone has thought of\. A new notes file could have any name\. And a check that only visits the approved files would never discover an extra one\.

This small JavaScript example shows the comparison with invented filenames\. The real checker also handles symbolic links and other release checks\.

```
const approved = new Set(['index.html', 'assets/site.css']);
const actual = ['index.html', 'assets/site.css', 'notes.txt'];

const unexpected = actual.filter(file => !approved.has(file));
const missing = [...approved].filter(file => !actual.includes(file));

if (unexpected.length || missing.length) {
  throw new Error('Output differs from approved file list');
}
```

![Build a clean output folder, list every file and compare with the approved list\. Stop on a mismatch\. A match proceeds to remaining release checks\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/release-file-check-flow-v2.svg)

The file inventory is one release check\. Matching filenames still need content and credential checks\.

## I added a file that should be rejected

For this article, I copied the current build into a temporary directory and checked the clean copy\. Then I added a harmless file called editorial\-notes\.txt at its root and ran the same checker again\.

I put it outside the reserved private folders so the test would reach the approved\-list comparison\. Otherwise a separate private\-folder rule might reject it first, leaving the comparison untested\.

The clean copy passed\. The copy containing the extra file failed\. These were the recorded results\.

```
Clean output accepted
Deploy artifact differs from positive allowlist
```

## What that result established

The check rejected the extra file in that temporary copy\. That gave me evidence about the behaviour I had asked the agents to implement\.

The short JavaScript example reaches the same kind of failure because notes\.txt appears in actual but not in approved\. Remove that extra filename and both lists match\. The code teaches the comparison\. The temporary\-directory check exercised the website’s actual checker\.

If a checker accepted the unwanted file, I would look at how it collected the inventory and whether a mismatch stopped publication\. If the checker rejected it but the build kept copying it, the copy step would need fixing\. Adding the file to the approved list just to get a pass would hide the problem\.

The approved list still needs maintenance\. When I deliberately add a public page or image, I update it as part of reviewing what will become public\.

## The result has to follow the release

I record the source revision checked and publish the reviewed output manually\. If an agent changes the build afterwards, the changed output needs checking again\. An earlier result describes the earlier version\.

After publication, I compare the local public text files with the files served by the website\. That answers a different question\. A correct build can be ready locally while the host still serves an older copy\.

The file inventory has a limit too\. A JavaScript file can have an approved name and still contain private information\. Content review, credential scanning and browser checks each cover further parts of the release\.

![Tests and review match revision A\. A later edit creates revision B, which needs its own review before release\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/ai-agent-revision-evidence-v4.webp)

A simplified illustration\. Evidence recorded for revision A does not establish that revision B has been checked\.

## A check to try on your next change

Choose one unwanted outcome the change must prevent\. Prepare an input that should trigger it, run the check and inspect what actually happened\. Keep the result with the version you checked\.

The same approach could help with a data pipeline\. Give it a sample with a required field missing, then inspect the published report as well as the job status\. A failure message would not be enough if malformed data had already reached the report\. This is a suggested application, rather than an incident from my work\.

For this website, the useful evidence was straightforward\. The same checker accepted the clean copy and rejected the copy containing an unapproved file\.

## About this note

Based on my personal website’s publishing checks\. The rejection result came from a temporary copy containing a harmless fixture\. The code is a simplified illustration with invented filenames\.

[Read on the website](https://mustafahafeez.com/blog/reviewing-ai-agent-work/)
